slides.text:
A string is bytes, but people think in characters. Go's answer is the **rune**: one character, kept as its Unicode number.

In this module you will do math with runes, count and walk text by characters, cut it without breaking a character, and reverse it. Changing case and searching come in `strings-package` and `unicode-package`.

Every character has a number in Unicode: `a` is 97 and `é` is 233. A rune is that number. Because runes are numbers, you can compare them and do math with them.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.

exercises.title: Any character is a rune
exercises.guide: A rune holds the number of a character, in any alphabet.

chunks.guide: An accented letter is still one rune, with its own number.
Characters from other alphabets work the same way, with bigger numbers.

exercises.title: Write a character by its number
exercises.guide: Write a character with its Unicode number instead of typing it.

chunks.guide: Inside a string, a backslash, a `u` and four hex digits make a character.

notes.text: Hex 00e9 is 233, the number of the letter é.

chunks.guide: The same escape works in a rune literal.
Both ways of writing the rune are the same number.

exercises.title: Math with runes
exercises.guide: Runes are numbers, so you can add and subtract them.

chunks.guide: Subtracting `'a'` gives the position of a letter in the alphabet, starting at 0.

notes.text: Distance from a: 0 for a, 2 for c.

chunks.guide: Add to a rune to get a later character. `string` turns it back into text.
To wrap around the alphabet, take the position, add one and keep the remainder of 26.

notes.text: Goes back to 0 after the last letter.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `'e' - 'a'` is the number 4, and it is not converted, so it prints as 4. One less than `'e'` is `'d'`, which `string` turns into text.

exercises.title: Is it a capital letter?
exercises.guide: Count the capital letters of a text by comparing runes.

chunks.guide: A counter for the capitals found.
Capitals are in order in Unicode, so a rune is a capital when it sits between `'A'` and `'Z'`.

notes.text: Compares the character's number with A's.

chunks.guide: Show the count.

exercises.title: Count the digits
exercises.guide: Count the digit characters of the text: those from the first digit to the last one.

slides.text:
UTF-8 stores a character in 1 to 4 bytes. Plain English letters take one byte, `é` takes two and `世` takes three.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
a  -> 1 byte
é  -> 2 bytes
世 -> 3 bytes

slides.text: `len` and indexes count bytes. To count characters, use the `unicode/utf8` package. To walk them, use `range`: it decodes one character at a time and tells you the byte where it starts.

exercises.title: Count characters
exercises.guide: `len` counts bytes. Count the characters instead.

chunks.guide: The imports, with `unicode/utf8`, are already in the file. The `ï` takes two bytes.
`utf8` can count the characters of a string.
Characters that take three bytes make the gap bigger.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: The text has 9 characters. In bytes, `é` takes 2 and each of the two others takes 3, so the 6 single-byte characters make 14 in all.

exercises.title: Bytes and characters
exercises.guide: Print the size of the name in bytes, then in characters.

exercises.title: Walk a string
exercises.guide: `range` visits the characters of a string, not its bytes.

chunks.guide: A string with an accented letter in the middle.
The position is the byte where each character starts, so it jumps over the two bytes of `ñ`.

notes.text: The byte position, then the character.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `a` takes byte 0 and `ñ` takes bytes 1 and 2, so `!` starts at byte 3. `range` gives byte positions, not character counts.

exercises.title: Count one character
exercises.guide: Count how many times a character appears in a text.

chunks.guide: The text and a counter.
Compare each rune with a rune literal. A loop over bytes would never find `ñ`, because it takes two.
Show the count.

slides.text:
A rune slice has one slot per character, so you can index it, cut it and change it without breaking anything. Cutting a string by bytes can land in the middle of a character and leave broken text.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
runes: [A] [ñ] [o]
  cut after 2 -> Añ
bytes: [A] [ñ1][ñ2] [o]
  cut after 2 -> A + half of ñ

exercises.title: A slice of runes
exercises.guide: Turn a string into a slice with one slot per character.

chunks.guide: Converting a string to `[]rune` makes a slice of its characters.

notes.text: A copy with one slot per character.

chunks.guide: Now `len` and the index count characters, not bytes.
Unlike a string, a rune slice can change in place. Convert it back to read it as text.

exercises.title: Pick a character
exercises.guide: Split the city into characters, then print how many there are and the second one.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    city := "Málaga"
    letters := []___(city)
    second := letters[___]
    fmt.Println(len(letters), string(second))
}

exercises.title: Cut in the middle of a character
exercises.guide: Check whether a cut leaves valid text.

chunks.guide: `ñ` takes two bytes, so cutting at byte 2 keeps it whole.

notes.text: True when every byte belongs to a whole character.

chunks.guide: Cutting at byte 1 splits `ñ` in half, and the text is broken.

exercises.title: Cut by characters
exercises.guide: Shorten a text by characters, never by bytes.

chunks.guide: To cut by characters, convert the text to runes first.
Keep the first 3 characters and add dots. It is safe even with `ñ`.
The last 5 characters count back from the length.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    s := "añ"
    r := []rune(s)
    fmt.Println(len(s), len(r), s[1])
}
exercises.explanation: The string has 3 bytes and 2 runes. `s[1]` is a byte, the first of the two bytes of `ñ` (195), not the rune number of `ñ` (241).

exercises.title: Reverse a text
exercises.guide: Write a function that reverses a text, accents included.

chunks.guide: The function turns the text into runes and back. The reversing goes in between.
Swap the first and last characters, then the next pair, up to the middle.

notes.text: Only half the pairs: swapping all would undo it.

chunks.guide: Reversing bytes would break `ñ`. Reversing runes does not.
